transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nandakumar (Redwood SE), Mike Torres (Helios CTO), Sara Patel (Helios SRE), Luis Gomez (ML Eng)

Auto-generated summary (short):
Quick weekly POC sync to review benchmark results vs Helios's current baseline provider (BaselineCloud). Discussed latency and throughput tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted options, tuning knobs (batching, quant, kv cache), and next steps for tail-latency tests and cost comparisons.

Topics:
- Baseline vs Redwood raw numbers (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec)
- Sequence length and prompt shape impact
- Cloud/GPU type differences and mapping
- Reliability and error patterns seen during stress tests
- Next steps: reruns, access, cost calc

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick check-in, is this still fine as a 45 minute sync?
[00:08] Mike: yeah that's good, we wanna go over the numbers you sent yesterday. I skimmed them but, uh, want to make sure we're all aligned.
[00:15] Priya: cool, I'll kick us off with the high-level findings then Jordan can follow on cost and next steps.
[00:20] Priya: so, in short, Redwood's dedicated pool with the recommended quant profile gave us roughly 18% lower p95 latency on our 512 token median workloads vs BaselineCloud on the same instance class. p50s were similar, p99 though is where it gets interesting, we saw a roughly 12% reduction but there's more variance in the tail when sequence length spikes.
[00:44] Sara: can you clarify "recommended quant profile" - you mean the 4-bit L4 quantization you suggested? sometimes the notes say 4-bit, sometimes 8-bit in the sheet.
[00:53] Priya: right, sorry, the primary runs used L4 int4-style quant (we labeled it l4-small in the sheet), we also ran 8-bit as a sanity check. 4-bit reduced memory pressure and allowed larger batch sizes but there is a small accuracy hit on one of your evaluation prompts, which Jordan flagged last week.
[01:10] Luis: that accuracy hit—was that with the reranker prompt or the long-context summarization?
[01:15] Priya: mostly the summarization set, especially prompts with lots of rare tokens. the reranker was fine.
[01:21] Jordan: just to add, we also instrumented KV cache warm vs cold. when KV cache is warm the tokens/sec jumped ~25% on average, and p50 improved by about 20%. p99 benefits but you still see spikes if many cold sessions arrive simultaneously.
[01:40] Mike: what's the baseline's behavior there? they do some caching, but it's mostly session-level, right?
[01:45] Priya: BaselineCloud has a more opaque caching layer, they do session affinity which helps, but we saw in your logs they evict earlier at roughly 8k total tokens which caused more cold-starts for the longer flows.
[01:58] Sara: there were a couple of failures in the stress run overnight where the model started throwing 500s under sustained bursts. did Redwood see any similar errors?
[02:05] Priya: in our stress replays we saw increased queueing and a few rate-limiter triggered 429s when the test exceeded the configured burst window. no internal 500s from the runtime in our cluster for the runs we shared.
[02:20] Jordan: and we included the raw logs link in the sheet, there's a short note about a misconfigured client timeout from one of the Helios test agents that caused an aborted stream which shows up as a 500 in your dashboard.
[02:33] Mike: oh right I saw that, we'll clean that up.
[02:36] 
[05:12] Priya: walking through the numbers table — p50 for Redwood dedicated (gpus: A100 equivalence) was 120ms on your 512 median prompt; BaselineCloud was 125ms. p95 Redwood 320ms vs Baseline 390ms. p99 Redwood 620ms vs Baseline 700ms. tokens/sec sustained: Redwood 420 tok/s vs Baseline 350 tok/s on the same nominal instance class. these are averages across three runs.
[05:42] Luis: 420 tokens per second—what batch size were you using there?
[05:46] Priya: that was with dynamic batching, target batch of 4, max 8. we also included a run with batch size 1 for low-latency which gives slightly better p50 but drops throughput.
[05:58] Luis: and the model variant—this was the 7B open checkpoint right? with some operator fusions?
[06:04] Priya: yes, the 7B open model, we applied the Redwood compilation pipeline that picks optimized kernels. sometimes the transcriber shows "red wood compilation" which is actually our optimizer, sorry for the doc noise.
[06:15] Sara: any differences in GPU utilization? we saw your A100 runs were more efficient but Baseline claimed they were on a newer Ampere refresh.
[06:23] Priya: Redwood's kernel choices resulted in higher sustained GPU SM utilization for these prompt shapes — roughly 68% average vs Baseline's 55% on their reported metrics. memory usage was lower on our setup due to quantization and better KV packing.
[06:38] 
[08:00] Jordan: couple of practical notes—cost calculations in the sheet assume a reserved/dedicated price for Redwood pools. there's a column that compares to BaselineCloud on a pay-as-you-go basis which favors them for very low throughput but flips when sustained load is expected.
[08:14] Mike: that's important — our POC target is sustained 10k requests/week, not just bursts, so reserved capacity could make sense. how flexible is burst capacity on Redwood Dedicated?
[08:23] Jordan: we offer configurable burst pools; you can set an autoscale policy that keeps baseline reserved and allows short bursts to use a pre-warmed pool. Priya can show exact config suggestions after we finalize the expected QPS.
[08:36] Priya: yeah I noted a suggested autoscale: min 2 nodes, target cpu/gpu util 65%, burst +1 node for 5 minutes up to 4 nodes. we can tune that to your SLOs.
[08:48] Mike: ok.

[12:10] Luis: one thing I wanted to call out—when we tested long sequences (2k tokens) the p99 for Redwood got closer to Baseline, sometimes slightly worse, likely due to attention memory patterns. have you seen that?
[12:22] Priya: yes, on 2k sequences the memory spills and KV growth can cause scheduling bumps. we saw p99 at ~1.8s on Redwood vs 1.7s on Baseline for pure long-context runs, but tokens/sec still favored Redwood. it's a tradeoff.
[12:36] Jordan: recommended mitigation is twofold: enable chunked attention where possible and route long-context sessions to slightly larger instances with more memory, or fall back to Baseline for specific long-tail flows while keeping Redwood for median traffic.
[12:49] Mike: route decisions can be done at the smart routing layer, right? by policy?
[12:52] Priya: exactly—smart routing can inspect sequence length or request tag and send to the node pool that best matches. we can demo that in the next session.

[18:00] Sara: another operational question — audit logs and encryption. Baseline had a simple KMS integration. do you have examples of KMS/HSM integration and audit retention options?
[18:12] Jordan: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we can push audit logs to your S3 or SIEM. for the POC we can enable S3 log exports for 90 days; enterprise retention is configurable. I'll attach the compliance sheet.
[18:24] Priya: we also noted your SOC 2 requirement—our attestation is in the security pack link we shared. sometimes the auto-transcript reads that as "sock two" which is amusing.

[22:30] Mike: quick question on failure modes. when you saw 429s in Redwood tests, were those client rate limiter settings or underlying queue saturation?
[22:38] Priya: mostly client-side rate limiter—the test harness dropped into a burst that exceeded the configured burst window. when we removed artificial limiter caps the runtime queued requests and increased latency but didn't return 429s. so it's tunable.

[25:00] Jordan: Okay let's talk about the next validation step we agreed — Priya to run the 99th percentile tail test with sequence lengths up to 2k on a dedicated 80GB GPU equivalent to reproduce the long-tail behavior. we'll also run mixed workloads with 10% long-context to see blended p99.
[25:18] Luis: please include the same seed prompts we provided earlier, that makes comparison apples-to-apples.
[25:22] Priya: yup, we'll use the Helios prompt set (you uploaded to the shared folder).

[30:40] Mike: cost question again — the cost delta you show looks like Redwood is slightly more expensive per token at small scales but cheaper at scale. is that mainly due to reserved discount?
[30:49] Jordan: yep and also better packing and feed-forward kernel efficiency which reduces tokens-per-second hardware hours. the spreadsheet breaks down per-hour GPU cost, tokens processed, and effective $/M tokens. I'll send that link.

[33:10] Sara: from an SRE POV—we need an SLA mention. if we go dedicated what uptime/latency SLAs are you able to commit to?
[33:18] Jordan: our Dedicated offering has SLA tiers; standard dedicated SLA is 99.9% with latency targets per model class; enterprise SLA options available for 99.95 and dedicated support. I'll include the SLA table in the follow-up.

[37:00] Priya: last thing on tuning — batching strategy depends on your latency budget. if you need <150ms p50 we'd recommend small batches and aggressively warmed KV caches. if you can tolerate higher p50 for throughput, go for batch 4 with dynamic batching and 4-bit quant.
[37:18] Luis: would you recommend dynamic batch or a forced fixed batch for our workload? we have many short chat-like requests and some long summarization.
[37:26] Priya: dynamic is usually best for mixed workloads; combine with policy-based routing so long summaries go to a separate pool.

[40:50] Jordan: quick recap — action items are in the sheet, Priya will re-run tail tests and batching sweep, Jordan will send cost breakdown and security docs, Helios will share final prompt distribution and open the test workspace.
[41:05] Mike: perfect. do we want to schedule a follow-up for next Wednesday?
[41:09] Jordan: yes let's tentatively set 2025-09-17 15:00 UTC. I'll send invite.
[41:16] Sara: thanks, that works for me.
[41:19] Luis: works. thanks all.
[41:22] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet link and logs.
[41:25] (call end)
